distinguishing_features: Active cathodic protection via a sacrificial anode array electrically shorted to the titanium anode bus, rather than passive barrier/coating upgrade

Galvanic (self-powered) sacrificial coupling that holds a cathodic protective potential on the titanium surface rather than chemistry dosing (Prior Art 1/2) or telemetry-only impedance inference (Prior Art 3)
Sacrificial electrode geometry deliberately sized and placed within ~5 mm of the Ti surface to minimize IR drop in high-conductivity anolyte
Design specified as an integrated anode-housing deliverable rather than an additive dosing schedule or a corrosion-detection algorithm
parsed.objective_technical_problem: Prevent corrosion/depassivation of the titanium anode coating in a high-chloride, high-pH, high-conductivity anolyte without replacing the anode with a noble-alloy material.
parsed.viable_reason: As written the mechanism is physically incoherent at the stated scale: chlor-alkali anodes operate anodically at ~1000 A/m², so galvanically shorting a Mg-Zr or Zn-In sacrificial anode to the anodic bus cannot impose a cathodic protective potential on the Ti surface, and the electrode would be consumed near-instantly (1011 A/m² requirement is far beyond any practical sacrificial-anode current density).
parsed.non_obvious_reason: Passive galvanic cathodic protection by shorted sacrificial anodes is a conventional corrosion-control technique, but its application to an actively driven anodic titanium coating is not an obvious routine extension of any of the cited prior arts (which are chemistry dosing or electrical telemetry), so the distinguishing mechanism itself is not an obvious step even though the underlying CP method is standard.
